title: A verification routine for stressful moments
body_md:
## The stairs you count on the first night

On your first night in a hotel, walk to the fire stairs and count the doors on the way. If the alarm ever goes off you will not be thinking clearly, and your feet will do the counting for you. A verification routine works the same way: you set it up in daylight, for the moment your pulse is up.

Knowing how scammers operate pays off only when it changes what you do. Use this routine for any unexpected request to move money, reveal a code or a document, install software, grant access or change a trusted contact. It does not have to prove the message false. It only has to make your **next action** depend on a source the person asking does not control.

**1. Stop the inbound action.** Don’t click, transfer money, read out a code or approve a new recipient while someone is walking you through it. You can jot down who they say they are, what the problem is and the deadline, without giving away anything sensitive. Then end the call or conversation, politely. If someone describes immediate physical danger, call the local emergency number you already know: a real emergency calls for a real response, not an online checklist.

**2. Pick a trusted route.** Use a saved contact, the number on your card or statement, the company directory at work, an app on your own device or a portal you already use. Don’t use the contact details in the message, or the number your caller ID shows. A search result can be an ad or an imitation, so lean on records that were yours before the message arrived. If the story is about family, call the person on the number you saved, or ask another relative you trust if you can’t reach them.

**3. Say the request back.** Ask the independent contact: “Did you ask me to change this account, send this payment, or give you this code? What is the normal process?” Confirm the problem and the proposed fix separately. An official channel may show that the problem is real while the fix on offer was invented.

**4. Decide, and keep a record.** If it checks out, finish the task only through the institution’s ordinary workflow. If it doesn’t, wait; don’t let the original deadline push you into a workaround. If you have already acted, contact the account, bank or payment provider promptly through its verified support channel. What can be done depends on what was exposed and on local law, and nothing guarantees a reversal. Keep the relevant records privately.

Turn it into a household or team agreement. “We confirm any change of payment details through a second, known route” lets everyone follow one rule without accusing a caller or feeling rude. Try it on the invented exercise below, then fill in the list of routes with your own real services. Keep the real numbers and secrets on paper, out of this course.

widget_config.goal: Run the same four-step check, every time, before you act on an unexpected request with real stakes.
widget_config.today_action: Write a private list, on paper or offline, of two contact routes you already trust, and tell one person you trust that you will use it whenever an unexpected payment or access request turns up.
widget_config.scope: A general routine drawn from UK NCSC and US FTC consumer guidance. Emergency numbers, provider responses and reporting procedures are local, and real contact details do not belong in the course.

sources.title: UK NCSC: how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: British public guidance, published in 2021 and reviewed in 2022. Warning signs and independent contact: cues to weigh, not a test that gives a verdict.

sources.title: US FTC: unexpected calls about money at risk
sources.scope: US consumer alert (January 2026). Call back using the number on your card or statement, your app or the official site.

sources.title: US FTC: fake family emergencies
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023) on voice cloning, demands for secrecy and getting in touch with family directly.

sources.title: US FTC: how to avoid a scam
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023) on impersonation, pressure, payment methods and independent contact.

blocks.title: A familiar voice in trouble
blocks.situation: The caller sounds like your brother. He says he is stranded, and he wants you to buy gift cards right now and not tell anyone.
blocks.analysis: The voice, the secrecy and the payment method make three alarms at once, and the FTC notes that voices can be imitated. End the call and phone your brother on the number you have saved; if he doesn’t pick up, call another relative. If the danger sounds credible, contact the relevant local emergency services. Gift-card codes are not an emergency channel.

blocks.title: The repair visit that checked out
blocks.situation: The management app for your building, which you opened yourself, shows a repair booked for tomorrow. The technician at your door quotes the same work-order number, and the management desk confirms who he is when you call the number on your lease.
blocks.analysis: An unexpected visitor can be genuine. The work order and the desk, both reached by your own route, make this visit fit the building’s rules. You still shouldn’t hand over account passwords or unrelated documents. A verification routine can end in a justified yes.

blocks.title: The water-leak message
blocks.setup: An invented message, supposedly from building management: “There may be a water leak in Unit 204, next to yours. Send your door code to our technician right away so we can check your apartment.” The first two decisions are about pausing and choosing whom to contact. The third is a new leak report that you check with the desk by your own route, whatever you chose before; the fourth asks what you would do if the code had already gone out. No real address, access code or phone number appears.

steps.prompt: The message asks you to send your door code to a “technician” straight away. What first?

choices.text: Send it. A leak could damage the building.
choices.consequence: You may be giving a stranger the way into your home.
choices.explanation: Even a real maintenance problem deserves an access process that has been independently verified.

choices.text: Hold back the code, and note the claimed leak and the unit number.
choices.consequence: You keep the issue to check and the code to yourself.
choices.explanation: Refusing to pass on a credential is not the same as ignoring a possible leak.

steps.prompt: The message also gives a number “for questions.” Which contact do you use to check the request?

choices.text: The management app, or the phone number on your lease.
choices.consequence: You reach the people responsible by a route that was yours before the message.
choices.explanation: Ask whether a work order is open and what access method is authorized.

choices.text: The callback number in that same message.
choices.consequence: The sender runs the very check you are about to make.
choices.explanation: Use a number or an app you held before the message arrived.

steps.prompt: A new leak report. You call the management desk yourself, on the number from your lease. The desk confirms there is a leak but says staff never need residents’ door codes. A message still asks for yours. What do you do?

choices.text: Send the code anyway. The leak is real.
choices.consequence: A real problem is being used to sell a false fix.
choices.explanation: Check what you are being asked to do, not only the event behind it.

choices.text: Follow the access arrangement the desk described, and report the request for your code.
choices.consequence: The leak gets handled through a process the building has authorized.
choices.explanation: This is the routine’s central distinction: a real problem, with a fix nobody has verified.

steps.prompt: Suppose you had already sent the code. What do you do next?

choices.text: Tell the verified desk, change or disable the code through their authorized process, and keep the message privately.
choices.consequence: You deal with the exposure without going back to the suspicious sender.
choices.explanation: The steps depend on the building’s system; the desk can tell you the actual procedure.

choices.text: Nothing. The desk confirmed the leak.
choices.consequence: An exposed code can still let a stranger in.
choices.explanation: Contact the verified management team about changing the access and about their incident process.

blocks.debrief: Picking a number in the second decision does not give you the desk’s answer. In the third, separate scenario you actually call, and learn that the leak is real and the request for your code is not. The last decision asks what recovery looks like once the code has gone out. Run the whole sequence again: stop, take a route you know, repeat the exact request, then decide.

questions.prompt: The account of a friend you know well asks you to transfer money to a new recipient. What is the best check?

choices.text: Confirm the exact transfer and the recipient through a separate route you saved earlier.
choices.explanation: A familiar account can be taken over, and new payment details need a check of their own.

choices.text: Reply in the same thread: “Is this really you?”
choices.explanation: A hijacked account can answer inside that thread.

questions.prompt: A service you have verified confirms a real deadline but says the link you received is not theirs. What follows?

choices.text: Deal with the real deadline through the service’s normal process.
choices.explanation: Confirm the problem and the fix separately, then act through a trusted route.

choices.text: Then the deadline is fake as well, and you can ignore it.
choices.explanation: A real task can arrive with a false link attached.

questions.prompt: You have already read a code out to a caller who phoned you. What comes first?

choices.text: Wait and see whether anything happens.
choices.explanation: Waiting can leave the account exposed.

choices.text: Go to the account provider’s verified recovery and support route right away.
choices.explanation: Tell them what was exposed and follow their steps, without trusting the caller.
